svg.aria-label: The TLS 1.3 handshake between Bob's laptop and example.org: ClientHello, ServerHello, the encrypted server messages, the client's Finished and the request

g.text: check the chain, the name, the signature, the MAC
and a 🔒 NewSessionTicket, for next time

ol.li: Bob’s laptop sends a ClientHello: “I speak TLS 1.3, here are the ciphers I know, I want example.org (the SNI, server name indication), and here’s my half of a Diffie–Hellman exchange (the key share)”. It’s not encrypted: there’s no key yet.

The server answers with a ServerHello: its choice of cipher, and its own key share. Now both sides do Chapter 31’s X25519, and get the same secret, which never crossed the network. From it, they derive handshake keys.

Everything else the server says is encrypted (🔒) with those keys: its settings, its certificate chain, a signature over the whole conversation so far, made with the private key that belongs to the certificate, and a Finished message: a MAC over everything, proving nothing was changed on the way.

Bob’s laptop checks all of it. Does the chain lead to a root it trusts? Is the certificate for example.org? Does the signature check out with the certificate’s public key? Is the MAC right? If anything fails, it hangs up.

Its own Finished goes back, and in the same breath, the actual HTTP request, encrypted with fresh application keys. The whole handshake cost one round trip before the request could leave. (TLS 1.2 took two.)
The answer comes back encrypted. The server often adds a session ticket: a note Bob can show next time, to skip most of this.

figure.figcaption: The TLS 1.3 handshake. The sizes are real, from this chapter’s lab talking to example.org. 🔒 means encrypted.
